title: Seed sampling in the South Africa Seed Industry

lessons.title: Seed lots and the sampling chain
lessons.html:
Why seed sampling is special

Seed is sold for planting, so its quality determines the farmer's crop. A seed laboratory tests only a few grams or a few hundred seeds, yet the result is applied to a whole seed lot that may weigh many tonnes. Sampling must therefore be done according to strict, internationally recognised rules so that results are reliable and can be compared between laboratories and countries.

Key terms

  • Seed lot: a specified, uniform quantity of seed, identified by a lot number, from which samples are taken. Maximum lot sizes per species are set in the rules.
  • Primary sample: a small portion taken from one point in the lot.
  • Composite sample: all primary samples combined.
  • Submitted sample: the sample sent to the laboratory, reduced from the composite sample.
  • Working sample: the portion the laboratory takes from the submitted sample for a specific test.

The rules that apply

In South Africa seed sampling and testing for certification and trade follow the International Seed Testing Association (ISTA) rules, together with national requirements under the Plant Improvement Act 53 of 1976 and its regulations. The South African National Seed Organisation (SANSOR) plays a central role in the industry, including in the certification scheme. Seed samplers must be trained and, where required, authorised.

Conditions for sampling a lot

  • The lot must be uniform; if it is obviously not, it should not be sampled as one lot.
  • Containers must be identified and marked with the lot number.
  • The lot must be arranged so that the sampler can reach the required containers.
  • The lot must not exceed the maximum size for the species.

Seed treatment hazards

Much seed is treated with fungicides or insecticides, often coloured. Wear gloves and a dust mask, do not eat, drink or smoke while sampling, wash hands afterwards and follow the label and safety data sheet.

lessons.title: Sampling methods and equipment
lessons.html:
Taking primary samples

The number of primary samples depends on the lot size and number of containers, as set out in the ISTA rules. Samples must be taken from different positions in containers (top, middle and bottom) and from containers spread across the lot.

Sampling instruments

InstrumentUse
Stick or sleeve trier (stick sampler)Long, compartmented tube inserted into bags or bulk to sample along its length
Nobbe trierShort pointed tube for sampling bags of free-flowing seed
Hand samplingFor chaffy or non-free-flowing seed such as some grasses that do not flow through triers
Automatic samplerTakes samples from a seed stream during processing

Reducing the sample

The composite sample is usually larger than needed and must be reduced to the submitted sample size using an approved method:

  • Mechanical dividers: riffle (soil) divider, conical divider or centrifugal divider.
  • Modified halving or spoon method for some species, as permitted by the rules.

Never reduce a sample by simply pouring off part of it.

Packing, sealing and sending

  1. Put the submitted sample in a clean, suitable container; use moisture-proof packaging if moisture will be tested.
  2. Seal so that the sample cannot be tampered with.
  3. Label with lot number, species, cultivar, sample number, date and sampler.
  4. Complete the sampling report or request form.
  5. Send promptly to the laboratory and store away from heat and damp meanwhile.

Integrity

The sampler must be independent of pressure to produce favourable results. Report any non-uniformity, damage or labelling problem rather than ignoring it.

Key points

  • Seed lot, primary, composite, submitted and working samples form the sampling chain.
  • Sampling follows ISTA rules and national requirements.
  • Use the right trier for the seed and sample from across the lot.
  • Reduce samples only with approved dividers or methods.
  • Seal, label and document samples; protect yourself from seed treatments.
